definitions.text: An equation of the form ax + b = 0 where ‘a’ and ‘b’ are constants, a ≠ 0 and ‘x’ is a variable, is called a linear equation in one variable. In linear equation, the highest power of the variable is always 1.

definitions.term: General form of linear equation in one variable
definitions.text: ax + b = 0 and a ≠ 0 is also called the general form of linear equation in one variable.

definitions.term: Solving a linear equation in one variable
definitions.text: Solving a linear equation in one variable means finding the value of the variable that makes the equation true. To solve the equation, the goal is to isolate the variable on one side of the equation and determine its value.

definitions.term: Operations that do not change the order of an inequality
definitions.text: The following operations will not affect the order of inequality while changing it to simpler equivalent form: (i) Adding or subtracting a constant to each side of it. ii) Multiplying or dividing each side by a positive constant.

definitions.term: Effect of multiplying or dividing by a negative constant
definitions.text: The order of an inequality is changed by multiplying or dividing each side by a negative constant.

Generally, a linear inequality in two variables x and y can be one of the following forms: ax + by < c;  ax + by > c;  ax + by ≤ c;  ax + by ≥ c Where a, b, c are constants and a, b are not both zero.
The regions (i) and (ii) are called half planes and the line ax + by = c is called the boundary of each half plane.

definitions.term: Solution of a linear inequality in x and y
definitions.text: A solution of a linear inequality in x and y is an ordered pair of numbers which satisfies the inequality.
Note that the linear equation ax + by = c is called "associated or corresponding equation" of each of the above-mentioned inequalities.

definitions.term: Solution region for a system of linear inequalities
definitions.text: The graph of a system of linear inequalities consists of the set of all ordered pairs (x, y) in the xy-plane which simultaneously satisfies all the inequalities in the system. To find the graph of such a system, we draw the graph of each inequality in the system on the same coordinate axes and then take intersection of all the graphs. The common region so obtained is called the solution region for the system of inequalities.

formulas.use: General form of a linear equation in one variable.

formulas.formula: ax + by < c; ax + by > c; ax + by ≤ c; ax + by ≥ c
formulas.use: General forms of linear inequalities in two variables.
Use as the associated equation to draw the boundary line of ax + by <, >, ≤ or ≥ c.

formulas.formula: x = 0 to find the y-intercept; y = 0 to find the x-intercept
formulas.use: Substitute these values in the boundary equation to find two points for drawing its line.
Write one-variable inequality solutions in interval notation; parentheses mean the endpoint is excluded and square brackets mean it is included.

formulas.formula: Multiply or divide both sides by a negative number ⇒ reverse the inequality sign
formulas.use: Use when isolating the variable if the operation involves a negative number.

formulas.formula: Strict inequality (> or <) ⇒ dashed boundary; inequality with equality (≥ or ≤) ⇒ solid boundary
formulas.use: Choose the correct boundary style when graphing an inequality in the xy-plane.

fullMarks: For a one-variable equation, show the same operation on both sides when adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing; then state the value of x clearly.
For an inequality, reverse the inequality sign whenever you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number.
On a real number line, use an open circle for < or > and a filled circle for ≤ or ≥; draw the ray in the correct direction.
For a graph in the xy-plane, first write the associated equation, find two points (often the intercepts), and draw the boundary accurately.
Use a dashed boundary for < or > and a solid boundary for ≤ or ≥, because equality means points on the line are included.
Test a point not on the boundary, usually (0, 0), in the original inequality; show whether it satisfies the inequality and shade the correct side.
For a system, graph every inequality on the same labelled axes and shade only the common region that satisfies all inequalities.
mistakes: Mistake: Keeping the inequality sign the same after dividing or multiplying by a negative number. Fix: Reverse the sign every time you do this.
Mistake: Using a filled circle for a strict inequality or an open circle for an inequality that includes equality. Fix: Use open for < or > and filled for ≤ or ≥.
Mistake: Drawing a solid line for every inequality. Fix: Use a dashed line for < or >, and a solid line for ≤ or ≥.

Mistake: Shading the side of a boundary line without checking it. Fix: Substitute a test point not on the line into the original inequality; shade its side if it works, otherwise shade the opposite side.
Mistake: Reversing the x- and y-intercepts. Fix: Set y = 0 to find the x-intercept and x = 0 to find the y-intercept; write each point in (x, y) order.
Mistake: For a system, shading the union of the two regions or leaving both full regions shaded. Fix: The solution is only the overlap that satisfies both inequalities.
Mistake: Losing a negative sign while removing brackets or combining fractions. Fix: Distribute signs carefully and check the final value in the original equation or inequality.

rubric.how: Award for linking either strict inequality symbol to a dashed line.

rubric.why: An inequality that includes equality uses a solid line.
rubric.description: States that the boundary is solid for ≥ or ≤.
rubric.how: Award for linking either inequality symbol with equality to a solid line.
